clue.text: A horse exercised on the beach

indicators.note: a horse being exercised is put through its paces and moved about, so the letters get moved about too

explanation.surface: A rider gallops a horse along the sands.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ashore is on land at the coast rather than out at sea, as on a beach.

clue.text: A launch at sea

parts.note: to float a company or an idea is to launch it

explanation.surface: A small motor boat is out on the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Launch' reads as the boat, but here it is the verb, as in launching a company on the stock market.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel that is afloat is on the water, in other words out at sea.

clue.text: Valet cheers wildly in a fortified manor house in Kent

indicators.note: cheering wildly means the letters are thrown about without order

explanation.surface: A manservant whoops with delight inside a stately home.
explanation.walkthrough: HEVER CASTLE in Kent, south-east England, was the childhood home of Anne Boleyn.
explanation.definitionFit: Hever Castle is a moated, fortified Tudor manor house in the county of Kent.

clue.text: Prompting involving a deposit

indicators.note: to involve something is to take it in, so one word wraps around the other

explanation.surface: Someone is nudged into paying a down payment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deposit' suggests money paid up front, but here it means what is left behind, like sediment.
explanation.definitionFit: A remainder is the residue left over, just as a deposit is matter left behind or settled out.

clue.text: Accompany European type around China's capital

indicators.note: around means one piece goes about the other, enclosing it

parts.note: a sort is a type or kind

indicators.note: a capital is the head letter of a word, so only the opening one is kept

explanation.surface: A continental traveller shows a visitor round Beijing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China's capital' looks like Beijing, but it is just the first letter of China.
explanation.definitionFit: To escort someone is to go along with them as a companion or guard.

clue.text: What a judge may do, in part, we hear, in court

definitions.note: a description of the action, standing for the verb phrase

indicators.note: we hear means take the sound of the word, not its spelling

parts.note: in part means to some extent
someone up before the magistrates is in court

explanation.surface: A judge's role in court, which we are told about partly at second hand.
explanation.walkthrough: To be 'up' before a judge is to appear in court as the accused.
explanation.definitionFit: At the end of a trial the judge sums up the evidence for the jury before they retire.

clue.text: Leaders of our Liberal Democrats, advanced in years

indicators.note: leaders are those at the front, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

parts.note: first letters of the three words

explanation.surface: The heads of a political party are getting on a bit.
explanation.walkthrough: The Liberal Democrats are a British political party.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone advanced in years is elderly, which is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Follow gang a lot, uneasily

indicators.note: something done uneasily is unsettled and disturbed, so the letters are disturbed too

explanation.surface: Someone nervously trails after a group of toughs.
explanation.definitionFit: To tag along is to accompany or follow someone, often uninvited.

clue.text: This crossword's written by a chap for one and all

parts.note: the puzzle's setter is called Everyman
Jack is a typical man's name, standing for any chap

explanation.surface: A self-referential note that this puzzle was set by a man for everybody to enjoy.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's pseudonym is the puzzle series name, Everyman.
explanation.definitionFit: Every man jack is an idiom meaning every single person, without exception.

clue.text: Saying attributed to one showing at Cruft's, proposing marriage?

definitions.text: Saying attributed to one showing at Cruft's, proposing marriage?

parts.words: Saying attributed to one showing at Cruft's
parts.note: surface reading: a remark made by an entrant at a dog show
setter's reading: a proverb asking a partner to accept you along with your pet

explanation.surface: A dog-show exhibitor pops the question.
explanation.walkthrough: Crufts is Britain's best-known dog show. The proverb means that whoever loves you must accept everything that comes with you.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb asks a suitor to take on a person's faults and attachments, pictured here as a pet dog.

clue.text: Tedious and ill-mannered youth's playing grand now inside

indicators.note: inside means one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a lout is an uncouth young man; the 's is read as has

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters are played about with and put in a new order

explanation.surface: A rude teenager bores everyone by playing the grand piano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grand' reads as a piano, but it is just letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Something long-drawn-out is prolonged beyond its interest, which makes it tedious.

clue.text: Put on trial, US soldier back in Scottish isle

indicators.note: in places one piece within the other

parts.note: Arran is an island in the Firth of Clyde

indicators.note: back means the soldier's letters are read the other way

explanation.surface: An American soldier returns to a Scottish island to face court proceedings.
explanation.definitionFit: To arraign someone is to bring them before a court to answer a charge.

clue.text: Artist needing help (a struggling Italian artist)

indicators.note: struggling suggests twisting and writhing, so the letters are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: A painter in difficulty asks for assistance.
explanation.walkthrough: The parenthesis makes the surface flow; 'Artist' gives the abbreviation RA, a member of the Royal Academy.
explanation.definitionFit: Raphael was the Italian Renaissance painter of Urbino, a master of the High Renaissance.

clue.text: Knowing one, extremely perceptive convict put on old group of islands

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes of the word, its first and last letters

parts.note: an old lag is a convict

explanation.surface: A shrewd inmate is described as very perceptive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on' is the down-clue joiner placing the convict above the final piece.
explanation.definitionFit: An archipelago is a chain or cluster of islands in one sea area.

clue.text: Ring foremost of botanists also

indicators.note: foremost means the one in front, so only the opening letter is kept

explanation.surface: Plant scientists also phone someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A band is a ring or hoop, such as a wedding band.

clue.text: Fellow taking taxi, forgetting bishop and monk

indicators.note: taking means one piece takes the other in

parts.note: a don is a university fellow

indicators.note: forgetting something means leaving it out, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: a minicab is a private hire taxi

explanation.surface: A college fellow hails a cab, leaving behind a bishop and a monk.
explanation.walkthrough: A minicab is a British private-hire car booked by phone rather than hailed.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dominican is a friar of the order founded by St Dominic, a kind of monk.

clue.text: Happy hour — binge in one next door

indicators.note: happy here means merry or tipsy, so the letters reel about out of order

explanation.surface: Cheap drinks lead to a drinking spree at the house next door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Happy hour' is a phrase, but 'Happy' is the signal and 'hour binge' is the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A neighbour is a person living in the next house.

clue.text: Writer has story about head of charming amulet

indicators.note: about means going round, so the story surrounds the letter
the head is the top, so just the opening letter is kept

explanation.surface: An author tells a tale about a lucky charm.
explanation.definitionFit: A pentacle is a five-pointed star figure worn or used as a magic charm, so an amulet.

clue.text: Wine and dine in harbour

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to host guests with food and drink
second meaning: to hold a thought or feeling in mind

explanation.surface: A dinner date takes place down by the docks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harbour' looks like a port, but it is the verb, as in harbouring a doubt.
explanation.definitionFit: You entertain guests at dinner, and you entertain or harbour an idea in your mind.

clue.text: Girl crushed by satirists

indicators.note: something crushed by a word is squeezed inside it, so look within the next word

explanation.surface: A young woman is humiliated by mocking comedians.
explanation.definitionFit: Iris is a woman's first name; crosswords often define names as girl or boy.

clue.text: Be given new deal — that's good for parish officer

indicators.note: something new is remade, so the letters are made into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A local church official welcomes a fresh agreement on pay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New deal' recalls Roosevelt's programme, but 'new' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A beadle was a minor officer of a parish who kept order in church.

clue.text: Crime of wicked senator

indicators.note: wicked suggests something twisted or corrupted, so the letters are twisted

explanation.surface: A corrupt politician's offence.
explanation.definitionFit: Treason is the crime of betraying one's country, the gravest offence against the state.

clue.text: Litter in saloon

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a covered chair carried on poles
second meaning: an enclosed car with a separate boot, as Americans call it

explanation.surface: Rubbish strewn about a bar.
explanation.walkthrough: A litter is a carried couch or chair, not rubbish; a saloon is the British name for a family car.
explanation.definitionFit: A sedan chair is a litter carried by bearers, and sedan is the American name for a saloon car.

clue.text: I could be given permission to enter running heat

definitions.text: I could be given permission to enter running heat

indicators.note: to enter something is to go into it, so one piece goes inside the other
running suggests letters in motion, moving into a new order

explanation.surface: A sprinter hopes to be allowed to compete in a qualifying race.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the answer speaking of itself: a runner who might be admitted to a heat. 'I could be given' just joins the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Only a competitor such as a runner would be granted entry to a race heat.

clue.text: Obscure bird? Boy rings any number in a fantastic place

indicators.note: rings means encircles, so the boy wraps around the number

parts.note: to cloud an issue is to obscure it
n stands for an unspecified number in maths

explanation.surface: A child phones round about a rare bird in some fairy-tale land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obscure bird' reads as one rare species, but it is two pieces: a verb and a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloud-cuckoo-land, from Aristophanes' Birds, is an imaginary realm of absurd fantasy.

clue.text: Some bourbon belonging to us

indicators.note: some means just a portion, so the answer is a part of the next word

explanation.surface: A share of the whiskey is ours.
explanation.definitionFit: The possessive word for things that belong to us.

clue.text: Doing wrong, English bishop and social worker

parts.note: ants are social insects and the classic worker

explanation.surface: An English bishop and a welfare officer behave badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Social worker' reads as a welfare job, but it is the insect, which lives in colonies.
explanation.definitionFit: Errant means straying from the right course, so erring or doing wrong.

clue.text: Bird, duck, on shimmering Loire

parts.note: a duck is a zero score in cricket, shaped like O

indicators.note: shimmering water breaks up its reflection, so the letters are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A duck and another bird on the glinting French river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' looks like the water bird, but it is cricket's score of nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: The oriole is a brightly coloured songbird, such as the golden oriole.
